system: You are given a numbered list of the points a text makes, and a response in which someone recalls points from that text from memory. Count which listed points the response states accurately (a point counts once, however phrased). Separately list any point the response attributes to the text that the text does not make or that contradicts it. Reply with JSON only: {"recalled": [point numbers], "inaccurate": ["..."]}

RESPONSE:
# The team note, recalled from memory

This is reconstructed without looking back, so the wording is approximate and some details may have drifted. Section 3 of the note is about exactly that risk, so anything that matters should be checked against the text.

**Title:** "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."

## Opening
- It is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice is what slips: under deadline, late in a long day, or when a confident colleague is in the room.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned
- This applies to claims from papers, colleagues, summaries and your own earlier notes.
- Don't give a claim more weight because it is fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Don't give it less because it is inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask what supports it, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.
- A well-measured result from a controlled comparison is heavy. A plausible mechanism suggested after the data were in is light but not nothing: note it and say what would test it.
- A confident sentence carries the weight of its evidence and no more. "Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world."
- Both errors are costly but not equally visible. Inflation is easy to spot afterwards; deflation is harder. A caveat added to a sound result looks careful but is a misreport.
- Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one.
- **Example:** a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If the evidence is three months of the supplier's own figures, say so and weigh it accordingly. If it is your own incoming inspection over a year, don't bury it under "it may be noise".

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer
- Take in all of it, and show that you have, by briefly restating the substance in your own terms.
- This isn't politeness. It is how both sides find out whether what was received matches what was sent.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to drop.
- A reply that handles three easy points and skips the hard fourth has answered a different, easier message.
- If you can't restate something, you haven't understood it, and the next move is a question.
- Then move on. The restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful part is the implication, the gap, or the next test.
- **Example:** a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Restate all five in a line each, answer four, and say the budget question needs figures you don't have yet and when you will have them.

## 3. Go to the source
- Summaries, abstracts, notes and memory are compressions. They lose the details that matter later: the denominator, the subgroup, the condition under which a result held.
- When a decision depends on a specific detail, check the primary material, not the summary or your recollection.
- This applies most to what you think you already know. Claims you have repeated to yourself are the most likely to have drifted.
- The source is the referee; agreement among colleagues is not. A team that checks claims against each other rather than the data can drift into a shared mistake that no one inside can see.
- **Example:** a report remembered as "costs fell 12%" actually said "costs per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%". Open it before citing it in a budget meeting.

## 4. Don't close what is open, and don't keep open what is closed
- Mark honestly which questions the evidence settles and which it leaves open.
- Closing early feels like progress, but it turns uncertainty into a false fact that others will build on. If a question is open, say so, say what would close it, and carry it forward.
- The mirror failure is keeping a settled question open out of discomfort or because one more check feels safer. That wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support. When the evidence has closed a question, close it, say why, and move on.
- **Example:** a new form reduced errors at two sites. Whether it works at the busiest site, which has a different workflow, is open. Report the first as found and the second as open, not the first as "promising" and the second as "likely".

## 5. Value the colleague who sees differently
- The most useful thing a colleague offers is what you couldn't produce yourself: an objection from a different starting point.
- A reviewer who knows exactly what you know mostly returns what you already see. Difference is where new information comes from.
- Protect that difference. Give the reviewer the material and the question, not your conclusion, your worries or your hopes. Sharing your view doesn't just bias them; it removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- When you are the fresh reader, read first and form your view before looking at others' conclusions.
- Raise objections when you have them. One held back because the room seems settled is information the team never gets.

## 6. Make your moves where they can be seen
- When you can see the right next step, take it and make it visible so others can check or reverse it.
- Share drafts before they feel finished. Make the call and show your reasoning. Push the result so someone can look at it.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence already settles hands it to someone with less context, and stalls the work on your guess about what they would say.
- Your guess about a colleague's response is your own model of them and contains nothing new. Only a real move gets a real reply.
- This is not licence to ignore others. Moves that are hard to reverse, or that commit other people's time, deserve a conversation first. Most moves are reversible, and for those the default is to make them openly.
- **Example:** instead of asking "should I restructure section three?", restructure it in a copy, say what changed and why, and invite reversal.

## 7. Failures come in pairs
Each correction tends to push toward its mirror, so know both sides:
- **Inflating / deflating** a claim.
- **Inventing a flaw / inventing a reassurance.** Finding problems that aren't there to look rigorous; dismissing real ones to keep things moving.
- **Closing too early / keeping open too long.**
- **Killing a live line / keeping a dead one.**
- **Deferring / dismissing.** Accepting a claim because of who made it; rejecting it for the same reason.
- **Offloading / overriding.** Asking others to decide what you can see; deciding alone what genuinely needs others' input.

If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.

## A last word
- None of this is a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes careful work when it goes well, and you will mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, the result that doesn't come out as expected. Welcome those.

**Confidence:** the structure, the examples and the six pairs I'm fairly sure of. The exact phrasing, and some of the reasoning I've attributed to particular sections, are paraphrase and could be blended between sections.
